Adam Smith. The Scottish economist and moral philosopher whose book The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, established the foundations of modern economics and capitalism itself.

Smith introduced an idea that would define the next two hundred years of economic thought: the concept of the invisible hand. He argued that individuals pursuing their own self-interest in a competitive market actually produce the greatest good for society. This was revolutionary in an age of mercantilism, when governments believed they needed to control trade and hoard precious metals to make nations wealthy. Smith showed that markets could self-regulate through competition without central government planning. This wasn't pure laissez-faire, though. Smith recognized that markets worked best when people were educated and moral, and he warned against monopolies and merchant cartels.

Smith's analysis of how economies actually worked was equally important. He distinguished between the natural price of something, determined by labor costs and materials and ordinary profit, and the market price, set by supply and demand. He was thinking about supply and demand curves two centuries before they were drawn on paper.

He believed the division of labor was the key to productivity. Specialization and dividing tasks into smaller pieces could increase output exponentially. His famous example was the pin factory. He showed that ten workers, when each specialized in one step, could produce forty-eight thousand pins a day. If each worker had to make whole pins, they'd produce only a few dozen. But Smith understood the human cost. Workers doing repetitive tasks day after day, without engaging their full mental capacities, could become intellectually deadened. So he championed education and public investment as necessary counterweights.

On trade between nations, Smith argued against mercantilism and protectionism. He showed that free trade allows each nation to specialize in what it produces most efficiently, increasing total wealth. This was the birth of international economics as we understand it. He held that government should minimize intervention in markets, though he carved out roles for public investment in infrastructure and education.

Before he was an economist, Smith was a moral philosopher. In his book The Theory of Moral Sentiments, published in 1759, he argued that sympathy, or empathy, is the foundation of all moral philosophy. This was the crucial move: Smith integrated his moral philosophy with his economics. Self-interest is not selfish vice. It's a natural human drive that, when properly channeled through market competition, serves the public good. His vision shifted how people thought about economies for centuries to come. Later economists from David Ricardo to John Stuart Mill built on his framework. Even Karl Marx, who rejected Smith's conclusions about capitalism, worked partly in dialogue with Smith's analysis. John Maynard Keynes later challenged Smith's assumption that markets automatically reach full employment. Yet Smith remained simultaneously celebrated as capitalism's intellectual godfather and contested as the originator of assumptions about human nature and market behavior that critics would later question.
